notes.headline: Disney: adjusted EPS up 59% in a quarter flattered by an extra week, with double-digit growth promised again
notes.takeaway: Revenue rose 16% to $25.9 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.77 beat the $1.68 consensus, against $1.11 a year ago. The quarter had 14 weeks instead of 13, which Disney says added about $0.17 to full-year earnings. Excluding it, fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS grew 16%, and the company again guided to double-digit growth in fiscal 2027.
results: Disney reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $25.9 billion, up 16% from $22.5 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $1.77 against $1.11 a year earlier and a consensus of about $1.68; reported EPS was $1.51 against $0.73. Total segment operating income rose 43% to $5.0 billion.

For the full fiscal year, revenue grew 8% to $102.3 billion, passing $100 billion for the first time, and segment operating income grew 12% to $19.7 billion. Adjusted EPS rose 18% to $7.02. Reported EPS fell 18% to $5.63, a decline that reflects one-off items in the comparison rather than the operations.

The quarter and the year included a 53rd week. Disney estimates the extra week added about $0.17 to full-year adjusted EPS; excluding it, the company says segment operating income grew about 10% and adjusted EPS about 16% for the year.
mgmt: In its letter to shareholders, Disney said it closed the year with a strong quarter, with 4% more guests at its parks and experiences worldwide and higher engagement on its streaming platforms and across ESPN, and that it exceeded its guidance for fourth-quarter segment operating income and full-year adjusted EPS.
Management described fiscal 2026 as a pivotal year delivered in what it called a challenging macroeconomic environment, and restated the company’s aim of compounding growth for shareholders.

For fiscal 2027 Disney continues to expect double-digit growth in adjusted EPS, excluding the effect of the 53rd week. It reminded investors that the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027 will be compared against this year’s 14-week quarter, which will make that quarter’s reported growth look weaker.
view: Start by removing the extra week, because the headline growth rates overstate what happened. A 14-week quarter against a 13-week quarter adds roughly 7% to revenue by itself, so 16% revenue growth is closer to 8% to 9% on a like-for-like basis. That is still a good quarter for a company of this size, and Disney deserves credit for stating the adjustment plainly, but investors comparing this report with the year-ago period should use the underlying figures: about 10% operating income growth and 16% EPS growth for the year.

Those underlying figures describe a company that has repaired itself. Two years ago the questions about Disney were whether streaming would ever make money, whether the parks had been over-priced into declining attendance, and who would run the company. Streaming is now profitable and growing, park attendance rose 4% globally, and earnings are compounding in the mid-teens. Sixteen per cent EPS growth excluding the extra week, on top of a strong prior year, is a rate few companies with $100 billion of revenue manage.

The parks number matters most. Experiences generates the majority of Disney’s profit, and attendance growth of 4% in an environment management itself calls challenging says pricing has not broken demand. Disney is also in the middle of a very large investment programme in parks and cruise ships, so capacity is still being added. The risk is the one it has always been: a consumer downturn hits a business selling expensive family holidays quickly, and the investment programme raises the fixed costs that would then need covering.

The shares barely moved, which is a fair reaction to a report that confirmed rather than changed the picture. The guidance — double-digit EPS growth again — was already expected, and the comparison in the final quarter of next year will optically slow reported growth. What would change the valuation is evidence that streaming margins can approach those of the best in the industry, and clarity on the long-term economics of ESPN as it moves from cable bundles to direct subscriptions. Neither was resolved here.
notes.watch: Streaming operating margin and park attendance through the December and March quarters. The first decides whether Disney is valued as a media company in decline or a streaming company on the rise; the second is the earliest indicator of consumer strain.
